whyChoose.title: Why Talk to an Attorney Soon

items.title: The Clock Is Running
items.desc: California generally gives you two years from the date of injury to file a claim, but claims against a government agency can require notice in as little as six months. Waiting too long can cost you the right to recover anything at all.

items.title: Fault Doesn't Have to Be Clean
items.desc: Under California's pure comparative fault rule, you can still recover damages even if you were partly responsible for what happened. Your compensation is simply reduced by your share of fault, not eliminated.

items.title: No Ceiling on Pain and Suffering
items.desc: California places no cap on non-economic damages, such as pain and suffering, in most ordinary injury cases. An attorney can help you understand what that means for your specific situation.

items.title: You Pay Nothing Upfront
items.desc: Attorneys in our network work on contingency, so there's no fee unless they recover money on your behalf. That means a consultation costs you nothing out of pocket.

items.question: How long do I have to file an injury claim in California?
items.answer: In most cases, California law gives you two years from the date of the injury to file a lawsuit. If your injury involves a government entity, such as a city vehicle, the notice window can be as short as six months, so it's important not to wait.

items.question: Where do crashes tend to cluster in Ione?
items.answer: Public records show that reported injury collisions in Ione have involved corridors such as Rt 104, Preston Avenue, Shakeley Lane, and W Main Street, with reports peaking on Thursdays between 3 and 5 p.m. This is simply a pattern in the public data, not a judgment about any particular road.

items.question: What if I was partly at fault for the accident?
items.answer: California follows a pure comparative fault rule, which means you can still pursue compensation even if you share some responsibility. Your recovery would be reduced by your percentage of fault, but it isn't automatically barred.

items.question: Is there a limit on how much I can recover for pain and suffering?
items.answer: No, California does not cap non-economic damages like pain and suffering in typical personal injury cases. An independent attorney can review your circumstances and explain what factors might affect your case.
